implementation_notes: Java's standard library supplies the containers but not the pattern: a Scope class holding a HashMap<String, Symbol> (or LinkedHashMap when diagnostic order must be stable) with a parent reference, or an ArrayDeque of scopes as the stack of open scopes, plus define/lookup methods that walk from the innermost scope outward. What replaces the classic structure is the Collections Framework and Java's type system - the roles become plain classes and the scope stack becomes a deque - while the define/resolve pass discipline stays yours. Keep the hand-written table for your language, DSL or tooling that must not depend on javac internals; when the language being analysed is Java, the JDK's compiler API already resolves names: Trees.getElement(TreePath) maps a use to its Element and Trees.getScope(TreePath) returns the enclosing Scope - the second variant.
pitfalls: ArrayDeque rejects null elements (push(null) throws NullPointerException): represent 'no symbol' by absence instead of storing nulls, and never push a null root scope.
HashMap gives no ordering, so duplicate and unresolved diagnostics come out in arbitrary order unless a LinkedHashMap is used; unstable diagnostics break golden tests.

The compiler API is not a generic table: Trees.getElement resolves only Java trees inside a JavacTask, and wrapping a custom language in javac's tree model to reuse it costs more than writing the deque-of-maps table.

variants.name: jdk.compiler Trees over a JavacTask
variants.implementation_notes: When the language under analysis is Java, the JDK ships the resolved model: from a JavacTask you obtain Trees, and Trees.getElement(TreePath) returns the Element a syntax node denotes while Trees.getScope(TreePath) returns the enclosing javax.lang.model Scope with its enclosing class/method and local elements; Trees.isAccessible completes the picture. What replaces the classic structure is javac's own symbol tables and scope stack, exposed through the supported com.sun.source API instead of the internal com.sun.tools.javac.code.Scope. The trade-offs are that only Java is resolved, a compilation task with a configured file manager and module path is required, and every edit invalidates the paths you resolved against.
pitfalls: TreePath is tree- and position-specific: after an edit the old paths are meaningless, so re-resolve from the new AST instead of caching TreePath objects.
The API must be used with the compilation task's own trees: mixing trees from one task with Trees.instance of another throws IllegalArgumentException.
